## Project overview

This project examines how food prices in the United States have changed over
the past decade using the Consumer Price Index (CPI). It explores three
questions: how food-price trends vary across categories, whether prices show
seasonal patterns, and how recent inflation compares with the Federal
Reserve's general 2% inflation target.

The CPI tracks changes over time in the prices consumers pay for a
representative basket of goods and services. This analysis focuses on food,
connecting national price trends to a familiar part of household budgets.

## Data and methods

The analysis combines monthly CPI data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor
Statistics with annual food-category CPI data from the U.S. Department of
Agriculture. The datasets were cleaned and reshaped in R using the tidyverse
to support comparisons over time and across food groups.

Month-over-month and year-over-year percentage changes were calculated to
describe short-term movement and longer-term inflation. Visualizations made
with ggplot2 were used to investigate seasonal patterns, compare food
categories, and show how food-price inflation changed relative to the 2%
benchmark.

## Key findings

- Food prices showed mild seasonal variation, tending to be higher earlier in
  the year.
- Overall inflation was near 2% before 2020, rose above 6% after 2020, and
  later moderated to around 3%.
- Inflation patterns varied by food category. Eggs were the most volatile of
  the categories examined, while many categories peaked around 2022 and
  declined afterward.

## Interpretation and limitations

The results show that food-price changes vary over time and across categories;
the overall inflation benchmark does not describe every food group equally.
The CPI is an index of average price change, so it does not represent the
exact grocery costs or buying patterns of every household. The analysis is
descriptive: it identifies trends and seasonal patterns but does not explain
their causes.
